item.title: Mainstream Open Source Licenses: From MIT to AGPL, How Engineers Choose
item.description: In September 2017, React switched overnight from BSD+Patents to MIT. The reason: the Apache Software Foundation put React’s license on its “do not depend on” list, and Automattic (WordPress’s parent) immediately announced it would stop rewriting its UI on React. Facebook couldn’t withstand the ecosystem pressure and folded. Seven years later, in March 2024, Redis moved its core from BSD 3-Clause to a dual RSALv2+SSPL license — within a week AWS, Google, and Oracle jointly forked Valkey to replace it.

item.title: From Redis Switching to BSL to the AGPL Revival: Source Available, AI, and the License Wars
item.description: In August 2023, HashiCorp moved Terraform, Vault, Consul, and all its core products from MPL 2.0 to BSL 1.1. The community erupted; a month later the Linux Foundation spearheaded a fork called OpenTofu. You’d think the story ends there — but in April 2024 IBM announced a $6.4 billion acquisition of HashiCorp, closing in February 2025, making HashiCorp a business unit under IBM’s Red Hat. The license-changing OSS company didn’t decline; it became an acquisition target.

item.title: Shipping an App to Every NAS and Router OS: Packaging and Listing Differences Across fnOS, ZSpace, UGREEN, Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS, OpenWrt, and iStoreOS
item.description: In October 2024, TrueNAS SCALE 24.10 “Electric Eel” ripped out its k3s backend and moved the entire app layer from Helm Charts to Docker Compose. Overnight, every old tutorial telling you to add a “custom train” to TrueNAS stopped working — 24.10 also deleted the “Add Catalog” button. That same year, fnOS, ZSpace, and UGREEN each launched or rebuilt their app centers: fnOS’s .fpk, UGREEN’s freshly opened developer portal in May 2026, all racing to build an app ecosystem.
